pass_a_gloss: But Heracleon into the same words says that the Samaritan woman has confessed gracefully the things said by him; for a prophet, he says, is only the one knowing all things, which not all know; but the prophet does not know all things. And he wants through the “Our fathers worshiped on this mountain” to be shown the worship of the nations before the law; and through the “You say that in Jerusalem” that of the Jews according to the law; and the Samaritan woman as having come to be outside the city of the will of God through ignorance and neglect of the necessary things to have committed fornication. But the things said are very easy to refute; for from where does he show that only the one knowing all things is a prophet, and that the prophet does not know all things?
pass_b_english: On the same words Heracleon says the Samaritan woman has fittingly confessed what Jesus said. A prophet, he claims, is only one who knows all things — which not everyone knows — and yet “the prophet does not know all things.”

By [[“Our fathers worshiped on this mountain” >> Bible:John 4:20]] he wants the pre-law worship of the nations; by [[“You say that in Jerusalem” >> Bible:John 4:20]] the Jews’ worship under the law. He casts the Samaritan woman as having left the city of God’s will through ignorance and neglect, and so fallen into fornication.
These claims are easy to overturn. Where has he shown that only the all-knowing one is a prophet, or that a prophet does not know all things?
